Managing data (second half) Data transformations

#Data transformations

Suppose you are considering the use of income as an input to your insurance model. The cost of living will vary from state to state, so what would be a high salary in one region could be barely enough to scrape by in another. Because of this, it might be more meaningful to normalize a customer’s income by the typical income in the area where they live. This is an example of a relatively simple (and common) transformation.

median_income_table <- readRDS("median_income.RDS")
head(median_income_table)
median_income_table
library(dplyr)
## 
## Attaching package: 'dplyr'
## The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
## 
##     filter, lag
## The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
## 
##     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
customer_data<-read.csv("custdata.csv")
training_prepared <- left_join(customer_data, median_income_table, by="state_of_res")
training_prepared<-   mutate(training_prepared,   income_normalized = income/median_income)
training_prepared
head(training_prepared[,c("income","median_income", "income_normalized")])
summary(training_prepared$income_normalized)

Benefits

  1. Puts the data in a comparable scale

    • Instead of raw ages like 25, 30, 50, you get values like 0.9, 1.05, 1.75, meaning:

      • 0.9 → 10% younger than average

      • 1.75 → 75% older than average

  2. Helps machine learning models

    • Many algorithms (linear regression, gradient descent–based models, neural networks) perform better when features have similar ranges.

    • Scaling avoids some features dominating others just because they have larger numerical values.

  3. Makes interpretation easier in ratios

    • The result is a relative measure — for example, 1.2 means “20% above the mean age.”

#Centering and scaling

mean_age <- mean(training_prepared$age)
sd_age <- sd(training_prepared$age)
training_prepared$scaled_age <- (training_prepared$age-mean_age) / sd_age
head(training_prepared)

  • Centers the data around zero

    • After transformation, the mean of scaled_age will be 0.

    • This removes the bias from large positive or negative raw values.

      • Puts variables on the same scale

    • After scaling, the standard deviation will be 1.

    • This is important in models (like regression, k-means, PCA, neural networks) that are sensitive to variable magnitudes.

    • Example: Without scaling, a variable measured in years and another in millimeters would have vastly different ranges, skewing results.

      • Improves numerical stability

    • Large values can cause computational issues in algorithms like gradient descent.

subset(training_prepared,abs(age-mean_age)<sd_age) %>% select(age, scaled_age) %>% head()
subset(training_prepared,abs(age-mean_age)>sd_age) %>% select(age, scaled_age) %>% head()
training_prepared |> head()

Ploting density function for income

ggplot(customer_data,aes(x=income))+geom_density()

ggplot(customer_data,aes(x=income))+geom_density()+scale_x_log10()
## Warning in transformation$transform(x): NaNs produced
## Warning in scale_x_log10(): log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.
## Warning: Removed 6856 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_density()`).

signedlog10 <- function(x) {
ifelse(abs(x) <= 1, 0, sign(x)*log10(abs(x)))
}

x=signedlog10(customer_data$income)
ggplot(mapping=aes(x=x))+geom_density()+scale_x_log10()
## Warning in transformation$transform(x): NaNs produced
## Warning in scale_x_log10(): log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.
## Warning: Removed 6874 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_density()`).

ordlog<-function(x){
  ifelse(x == 0, 0, sign(x)*log10(abs(x)))
}
x=ordlog(customer_data$income)
ggplot(mapping=aes(x=x))+geom_density()+scale_x_log10()
## Warning in transformation$transform(x): NaNs produced
## Warning in scale_x_log10(): log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.
## Warning: Removed 6874 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_density()`).

It’s also generally a good idea to log transform data containing values that range over several orders of magnitude, for example, the population of towns and cities, which may range from a few hundred to several million. One reason for this is that modeling techniques often have a difficult time with very wide data ranges. Another reason is because such data often comes from multiplicative processes rather than from an additive one, so log units are in some sense more natural.
